title: Location and Relations of the Endocrine Glands
subject: Endocrine System (ENDO)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter places the thyroid, parathyroid, pituitary, and adrenal glands in the body and explains what lies around each one. The neighbors matter more than the glands themselves on the exam: a question describes hoarseness or a lost high note after thyroid surgery, tingling and cramps the next day, loss of both temporal visual fields, or a difficult right adrenal dissection, and asks you to name the structure involved. If you can explain why the thyroid rises on swallowing, which nerve controls which laryngeal muscle, why the inferior parathyroids wander, what surrounds the sella, and how the two adrenals differ, you can reason through these questions instead of memorizing them.

connections.how: Third and fourth pouch migration explains why the inferior parathyroids are variable and the superior ones are constant.
The superior and inferior thyroid arteries are the landmarks for the two laryngeal nerves, and the short right adrenal vein shapes adrenal surgery.
Parathyroid hormone and the hypothalamic-pituitary portal system explain the hypocalcemia and stalk effect described here.
Pituitary adenomas, parathyroid adenomas, and adrenal masses produce mass effects predicted by the relations in this chapter.
The optic chiasm, cavernous sinus cranial nerves, and vagal branches to the larynx link this chapter to the visual pathway and cranial nerve anatomy.

terms.def: The visceral layer of deep cervical fascia that encloses the thyroid, trachea, and esophagus and binds the thyroid to the larynx and trachea.
The narrow band of thyroid tissue that joins the two lobes across the front of the second and third tracheal rings.
An inconstant upward extension of thyroid tissue from the isthmus, a remnant of the thyroglossal duct.
The furrow between the trachea and esophagus in which the recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends behind the thyroid lobe.
The only intrinsic laryngeal muscle supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; it tilts the thyroid cartilage to lengthen and tense the vocal folds.
The only muscle that abducts the vocal folds and opens the glottis; it is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
The saddle-shaped depression on the upper surface of the sphenoid body whose central hypophyseal fossa holds the pituitary.
A circular fold of dura that roofs the sella turcica, with a central opening for the pituitary stalk.
A paired dural venous sinus beside the sella containing the internal carotid artery and the abducens nerve, with cranial nerves III, IV, V1, and V2 in its lateral wall.
Loss of the temporal half of the visual field in both eyes, caused by damage to crossing nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm.
The fibroareolar sheath that encloses each kidney, its perirenal fat, and the adrenal gland, with a thin septum between adrenal and kidney.
Lying behind the parietal peritoneum on the posterior abdominal wall, covered by peritoneum only on the front.

sections.title: The thyroid: position, fascial sheath, and movement on swallowing

blocks.text: The thyroid is the largest purely endocrine gland, weighing about 15 to 25 g in adults. Its two lobes lie on either side of the lower larynx and upper trachea, each extending from about the level of the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage down to about the sixth tracheal ring. The isthmus joins the lobes across the front of the trachea, usually anterior to the second and third tracheal rings. In roughly half of people a pyramidal lobe rises from the isthmus toward the hyoid, marking the path of the thyroglossal duct along which the gland descended (EN-1).

The gland has its own thin fibrous capsule, which sends septa into the parenchyma. Outside this lies a looser sheath formed by the pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia, the visceral layer that also wraps the trachea and esophagus. Posteromedially the sheath thickens into a suspensory ligament that anchors each lobe to the cricoid cartilage and upper tracheal rings.

blocks.title: Relations of the thyroid
rows: Infrahyoid (strap) muscles, investing fascia, platysma, skin
Sternothyroid attaches to the oblique line and stops a goiter rising, so enlargement extends down behind the sternum
Carotid sheath: common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve
A large lobe displaces the sheath laterally
A goiter can compress or deviate the trachea (stridor) or esophagus (dysphagia)
Recurrent laryngeal nerve in the tracheoesophageal groove; parathyroid glands
Nerve and parathyroids are at risk in thyroid surgery (C02, C03)
blocks.caption: The thyroid sits in the visceral compartment of the neck, enclosed with the airway and gut tube.

blocks.title: Why a thyroid mass rises on swallowing
steps: Pharyngeal phase of swallowing begins
Suprahyoid and thyrohyoid muscles elevate hyoid and larynx
Pretracheal fascia and suspensory ligament tie thyroid to larynx
Thyroid and any mass within it move upward
Gland descends again as the larynx returns
blocks.caption: Movement on swallowing places a mass in the thyroid or in a structure fixed to the larynx.

blocks.text: This makes swallowing a bedside localizing test. A thyroid nodule or goiter rises when the patient swallows, whereas an enlarged lymph node in the carotid sheath or the lateral neck usually does not, because it lies outside the pretracheal fascia. A thyroglossal duct cyst is also tethered to the larynx through the hyoid and so rises on swallowing, but it is usually midline near the hyoid and, unlike a thyroid nodule, also rises when the tongue is protruded because of its tract toward the foramen cecum. A thyroid cancer that has invaded surrounding muscle or the trachea may become fixed and lose this mobility.

The same anatomy explains several other findings. Because the sternothyroid muscles cap the gland above, a large goiter grows downward into the superior mediastinum as a retrosternal goiter, where it can compress the trachea and great veins. The isthmus lies over the upper tracheal rings, so it is encountered in a tracheostomy, and an inconstant thyroid ima artery, present in a small minority of people, may ascend on the front of the trachea to the isthmus.

blocks.predict: A firm lateral neck mass does not move when the patient swallows or protrudes the tongue. Is it likely to be thyroid?
blocks.explain: Probably not. Thyroid tissue is bound to the larynx by the pretracheal fascia, so it rises with swallowing. A mass that does not move is more likely a lymph node or other structure outside that sheath, unless it is a thyroid cancer that has become fixed to surrounding tissue.

sections.title: The laryngeal nerves and voice changes after thyroid surgery

blocks.text: Two branches of the vagus nerve pass close to the thyroid, and they divide the work of the larynx between them. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies every intrinsic laryngeal muscle except the cricothyroid, so it controls opening and closing of the glottis, and it carries sensation below the vocal folds. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies only the cricothyroid, which tilts the thyroid cartilage forward on the cricoid, lengthening and tensing the vocal folds to raise pitch.

The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery; the left hooks under the aortic arch behind the ligamentum arteriosum, giving it a longer thoracic course. Both ascend in or near the tracheoesophageal groove behind the thyroid lobe, cross close to the inferior thyroid artery (in front of, behind, or between its branches, which varies), and enter the larynx deep to the inferior constrictor near the cricothyroid joint, where the suspensory ligament binds them tightly to the gland. In under 1% of people the right nerve is non-recurrent, running directly from the vagus to the larynx, usually with an aberrant right subclavian artery.

The superior laryngeal nerve divides high in the neck. Its internal branch pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to carry sensation above the vocal folds; its external branch descends alongside the superior thyroid artery to the cricothyroid. Each nerve therefore travels with a thyroid artery, and ligating those vessels is where injury occurs.

blocks.title: Nerve injury during thyroidectomy
rows: Inferior thyroid artery, suspensory ligament, tracheoesophageal groove
All intrinsic muscles on that side except cricothyroid
Fold fixed near the midline; hoarse, breathy, weak voice and weak cough; aspiration of liquids possible
All abductors and adductors except cricothyroids
Both folds near the midline; inspiratory stridor and airway obstruction; voice may sound fairly normal
Superior thyroid artery at the upper pole
Weak, monotone voice that tires easily; loss of high pitch
Thyrohyoid membrane, above the operative field
Loss of supraglottic sensation and cough reflex; aspiration
blocks.caption: The recurrent nerve controls glottic opening and closing; the external branch controls vocal fold tension.

blocks.title: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury
steps: Inferior thyroid artery branches ligated near the lower pole
Adjacent recurrent nerve cut, clamped, stretched, or heated
Intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid denervated
Fold cannot abduct or fully adduct; rests near midline
Unilateral: incomplete closure, hoarse breathy voice
Bilateral: glottis cannot open, stridor and obstruction
blocks.caption: Stretch or heat often causes temporary injury; transection causes permanent paralysis.

blocks.text: Because the posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor, the two injuries differ. With one nerve lost, the paralyzed fold rests near the midline and the opposite fold still opens the airway, but the glottis cannot close firmly, so the voice is hoarse and breathy. With both nerves lost, neither fold can open: the voice may be acceptable while the airway is dangerously narrow, typically recognized as stridor after extubation. Thyroid cancer, mediastinal tumors, an enlarged left atrium, or an aortic arch aneurysm cause the same hoarseness, more often on the left because of its longer course.

blocks.title: Predicting the nerve from the voice
blocks.text: A singer has a total thyroidectomy. Afterward she speaks clearly and breathes normally, but cannot reach high notes and her voice tires by evening. Normal breathing and loudness mean the recurrent nerves are intact. Pitch depends on vocal fold tension from the cricothyroid, so the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve was injured, likely while the superior thyroid vessels were ligated. A second patient who is hoarse and breathy with a weak cough has one fold that cannot close: one recurrent nerve. A third with a near-normal voice but noisy inspiration after extubation has bilateral recurrent nerve injury and an airway emergency.

sections.title: The parathyroid glands and their variable position

blocks.text: Most people have four parathyroid glands, each a flattened yellow-brown body about 5 to 6 mm long weighing about 30 to 50 mg. They usually lie on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes, outside the thyroid capsule but within its fascial sheath, and are easily mistaken for fat, lymph nodes, or thyroid nodules. A minority of people have five or more, and a few have fewer than four. Both pairs are usually supplied mainly by the inferior thyroid artery (EN-4).

Position is set by embryology, and the names involve a reversal. The inferior parathyroids arise from the third pharyngeal pouch with the thymus, which pulls them down as it migrates toward the mediastinum, so they end up below the glands from the fourth pouch. Because they can separate from the thymus anywhere along that path, they are the variable pair. The superior glands, from the fourth pouch, move only a short distance and stay fairly constant.

blocks.title: Superior versus inferior parathyroid glands
rows: Third pharyngeal pouch, with the thymus
Posterior thyroid lobe near the level of the cricoid cartilage, close to where the recurrent nerve enters the larynx
Near the lower pole of the thyroid lobe
Fairly constant; occasionally behind the pharynx or esophagus
Highly variable: thyrothymic tissue, thymus, anterior mediastinum, carotid sheath, or high in the neck if undescended
blocks.caption: Longer migration with the thymus makes the inferior glands the ones most often ectopic.

blocks.text: Variable position matters in two opposite operations. In thyroidectomy the parathyroids and their small arteries must be preserved, or parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion stops. In surgery for primary hyperparathyroidism an overactive gland, usually a single adenoma, must be found; an ectopic adenoma, most often an inferior gland in the thymus or anterior mediastinum, is easily missed, leaving PTH and calcium high. This is why the glands are localized by imaging, such as sestamibi scanning or ultrasound, beforehand.

blocks.title: From thyroidectomy to hypocalcemia
steps: Parathyroids removed, bruised, or devascularized
PTH secretion falls; circulating PTH clears within minutes
Less bone resorption and renal Ca2+ reabsorption
Less calcitriol, so less intestinal Ca2+ absorption
Plasma Ca2+ falls over one to three days
Neuromuscular excitability rises: tingling, spasm, tetany
blocks.caption: Low PTH also lets renal phosphate reabsorption rise, so phosphate is high.

blocks.text: The symptoms follow from a membrane effect. Extracellular Ca2+ binds the outer membrane surface and stabilizes voltage-gated Na+ channels; when ionized Ca2+ falls, they activate at a membrane potential closer to rest, so nerves fire spontaneously. The result is perioral and fingertip tingling, cramps, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, and in severe cases seizures. Tapping the facial nerve in front of the ear makes facial muscles twitch (Chvostek sign), and a blood pressure cuff inflated above systolic pressure for a few minutes provokes carpal spasm (Trousseau sign). The ventricular action potential plateau lengthens, prolonging the QT interval. Normal total serum calcium is about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL (2.1 to 2.6 mmol/L); ionized calcium is about 4.5 to 5.3 mg/dL (1.1 to 1.3 mmol/L).

blocks.predict: After removal of what looked like a single enlarged inferior parathyroid, a patient's calcium stays high. Where should the missing adenoma be sought, and why there?
blocks.explain: In the path of the third pouch: the thymus, the anterior mediastinum, the thyrothymic tissue, or the carotid sheath. The inferior glands migrate with the thymus and can stop anywhere along that route, so an abnormal gland may not be at the lower thyroid pole. A supernumerary gland is another possibility.

sections.title: The pituitary in the sella turcica and its neighbors

blocks.text: The pituitary, about 1 cm across and about 0.5 to 0.6 g, hangs from the hypothalamus by the infundibulum (stalk). It sits in the hypophyseal fossa of the sella turcica on the sphenoid body, between the tuberculum sellae in front and the dorsum sellae behind. The diaphragma sellae, a circular dural fold, roofs the fossa, with a central opening for the stalk. Stretching of this pain-sensitive dura is one reason a pituitary mass causes headache.

blocks.title: Neighbors of the pituitary and the effect of tumor extension
rows: Optic chiasm, just above the diaphragma sellae and in front of the stalk
Bitemporal visual field loss, starting in the upper temporal quadrants
Mild hyperprolactinemia from lost dopamine delivery (stalk effect); hydrocephalus if the mass is very large
Cavernous sinus: internal carotid artery and CN VI within; CN III, IV, V1, V2 in the lateral wall
Double vision, ptosis, a dilated pupil, and numbness of the forehead or cheek
Thin bony floor; the route of transsphenoidal surgery
Compression causes loss of pituitary hormones (hypopituitarism)
blocks.caption: Bone forms the floor and front and back walls; the dural roof and side walls yield, so a tumor grows upward and sideways.

blocks.text: Fibers from the nasal half of each retina, which see the temporal visual field, cross in the chiasm; temporal retinal fibers do not. A mass pressing on the center of the chiasm damages only crossing fibers, so the temporal field is lost in both eyes: bitemporal hemianopia. Inferior nasal fibers, serving the upper temporal fields, cross in the lower chiasm, so a pituitary tumor pushing from below usually takes the upper temporal quadrants first. A craniopharyngioma, often arising above the sella from Rathke pouch remnants, tends to take the lower quadrants first. A lesion of one optic tract, behind the chiasm, causes homonymous hemianopia instead.

blocks.title: Pituitary macroadenoma to bitemporal hemianopia
steps: Adenoma of 10 mm or more fills the sella
Bony floor resists; dural roof and side walls yield
Mass rises above the sella
Optic chiasm compressed from below
Crossing inferior nasal fibers fail first
Upper temporal quadrants lost, then full bitemporal hemianopia
blocks.caption: A microadenoma (under 10 mm) is usually too small to cause mass effect.

blocks.text: Lateral extension into the cavernous sinus compresses cranial nerves III, IV, and VI, causing diplopia, with ptosis and a dilated pupil when III is involved, and V1 and V2, causing facial numbness. The thick-walled internal carotid artery is often encased but rarely narrowed. Sudden hemorrhage or infarction into an adenoma (pituitary apoplexy) produces severe headache, visual loss, and ophthalmoplegia together. Diabetes insipidus is uncommon with adenomas, because vasopressin is made in the hypothalamus and can still be released above the compression; it suggests a hypothalamic or stalk lesion such as a craniopharyngioma.

blocks.title: Reading the field defect
blocks.text: A 45-year-old man bumps into door frames on both sides. Both eyes have lost their upper temporal quadrants, and his prolactin is mildly raised. Temporal loss in both eyes places the lesion at the chiasm, where crossing nasal fibers run. Upper quadrants first means compression from below, pointing to the pituitary rather than a mass above the chiasm. A mildly raised prolactin with a large mass suggests the stalk effect, a nonfunctioning adenoma interrupting dopamine flow in the portal vessels, rather than a prolactinoma, which usually raises prolactin far higher. Later diplopia and a drooping lid would mean lateral extension into the cavernous sinus.

sections.title: The adrenal glands: position and right versus left differences

blocks.text: The adrenal (suprarenal) glands are retroperitoneal organs on the posterior abdominal wall, each weighing about 4 to 5 g in adults. They lie on the superomedial aspect of the kidneys at about the level of the eleventh and twelfth thoracic vertebrae, resting posteriorly on the crura of the diaphragm. Each gland is enclosed within the renal fascia and surrounded by perirenal fat, but a thin fascial septum separates it from the kidney. Each has an outer cortex, derived from mesoderm, and an inner medulla, derived from neural crest (EN-1, EN-2).

Because the gland has its own fascial compartment and develops separately from the kidney, it stays in place when the kidney does not: a pelvic kidney leaves the adrenal in its normal position, and a kidney can be removed while the adrenal is left behind.

blocks.title: Right versus left adrenal gland
rows: Along the medial border from the superior pole toward the hilum
Inferior vena cava medially; bare area of the liver laterally
Stomach across the omental bursa, body of the pancreas, splenic vessels
Very short vein directly into the posterior inferior vena cava
Longer vein into the left renal vein, often joined by the left inferior phrenic vein
blocks.caption: Neighbors explain both the shapes and the difference in surgical difficulty.

blocks.text: The asymmetry has practical consequences. The right adrenal lies behind the inferior vena cava, partly hidden by it and wedged against the liver, and its vein is only a few millimeters long before it enters the cava. Dissecting the right gland therefore risks tearing the caval wall, and catheterizing that short vein for adrenal venous sampling is technically harder on the right. The left gland is reached behind the stomach and pancreas, and its vein drains into the left renal vein, which crosses in front of the aorta; this longer route makes the left vein easier to identify and sample.

Each gland receives many small arteries from three sources, the inferior phrenic artery, the aorta, and the renal artery, but drains through a single vein (EN-4). Its close relation to the kidney, liver, and vena cava also explains why adrenal masses are often found incidentally on abdominal imaging done for other reasons, and why a large right adrenal mass can push the liver forward or invade the cava.

blocks.predict: During removal of a right adrenal tumor, sudden heavy venous bleeding occurs. Which vessel is most likely injured, and why is the right side more vulnerable than the left?
blocks.explain: The inferior vena cava, at the entry of the right adrenal vein. The right vein is very short and enters the posterior cava directly, so traction on the gland tears the caval wall. The left vein is longer and drains into the left renal vein, away from the cava.

integration.text: Embryology explains most of these relations. The thyroid descends from the tongue base and stays bound to the airway by the pretracheal fascia, so it moves with the larynx. The long thymic migration of the third pouch makes the inferior parathyroids the variable pair. The recurrent laryngeal nerves first hook under the sixth arch arteries. On the right the distal sixth and fifth arch arteries regress, so the nerve rises to hook under the right subclavian artery, a fourth arch derivative; on the left the sixth arch persists as the ductus arteriosus, so the nerve stays under the arch at the ligamentum arteriosum. When the right subclavian arises aberrantly from the distal arch, nothing holds the right nerve down, and it is non-recurrent. The adrenal cortex and medulla form separately from the kidney, so the gland keeps its place when the kidney is displaced.

Physiology and pathology then turn anatomy into presentations. Loss of the cricothyroid changes pitch, loss of the posterior cricoarytenoid threatens the airway, loss of the parathyroids removes PTH and lowers ionized calcium until nerves fire spontaneously, and compression of the chiasm or stalk produces field loss and mild hyperprolactinemia. These rules have limits: relations of the recurrent nerve to the inferior thyroid artery vary widely, parathyroid number and position are inconstant, and the chiasm can sit forward or backward over the sella, so a classic pattern supports localization but does not prove it.

summary: The thyroid isthmus lies over tracheal rings 2 and 3; the lobes flank the larynx and trachea within the pretracheal fascia.
Fascial and ligamentous attachment to the larynx makes the thyroid rise on swallowing; a thyroglossal duct cyst also rises on tongue protrusion.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove near the inferior thyroid artery and supplies every intrinsic laryngeal muscle except the cricothyroid.
Unilateral recurrent nerve injury causes hoarseness; bilateral injury leaves both folds near the midline with stridor, because the posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor.
The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery to the cricothyroid; injury causes a monotone voice and loss of high pitch.
Inferior parathyroids come from the third pouch and migrate with the thymus, so they are the variable pair; superior ones from the fourth pouch are constant.
Parathyroid loss at thyroidectomy lowers PTH and ionized calcium, raising neuromuscular excitability and prolonging the QT interval.
The pituitary sits in the sella beneath the diaphragma sellae, with the optic chiasm above, the cavernous sinuses lateral, and the sphenoid sinus below.
Upward pituitary extension compresses crossing nasal fibers, causing bitemporal hemianopia that begins in the upper temporal quadrants.
The right adrenal is pyramidal, behind the IVC, with a short vein into the cava; the left is crescentic on the medial kidney border and drains to the left renal vein.

The frequency of supernumerary parathyroid glands is quoted from about 5% to over 10% depending on autopsy or surgical series; confirm the figure NABNE expects, if any.
A non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve is quoted at well under 1% to about 1%; confirm the value if tested.
